title: A rant on the notion of objectivity

commenti.body: Subjectivity is our initial human perception and first impression, which is always colored deeply by the individual's learned or adopted biases and preferences. Objectivity must be built upon multiple analyses of the similarities between several works. Objectivity normally requires the study of many examples, and identifying causes and effects in our perceptions. And even so, no matter how strong the correlation between those causes and their effects, there will always exist individuals who are not affected in the majority manner by a given work or element within it. Art is always therefore ultimately subjective. "Most people are likely to find.." is the most that any objective analysys of art can conclude.

>"Most people are likely to find.."

I feel as if even this is not exactly objective. It does not truly tell us anything about the work of art itself, but our reaction to it. There doesn't seem to me to be anything to suggest that because something is the consensus, or the conventional perspective, that this elevates it beyond subjectivity. If most people like logicality in their films, I think that the only thing this tells us, is that this is simply what most *subjects* prefer, and not what should constitute the objective consideration or criteria of art. If that makes any sense.

Its not so much that film criticism is or isn't objective, its that even if someone likes or dislikes a film for reasons you want to argue are not objective...that's all fine and well, but its very unlikely to actually change that person's view of any given film.

So, even if objectivity in film criticism were to exist, it would still be rendered *effectivelly* subjective. Because we can't begin to make the argument that a person didn't like a film that they say they did, or vice versa.

I agree with that, but I think that the goal of objectivists is to ignore entirely what other people think, and to essentially render different perspective of lesser truth and therefore inferior. They make a strict division between what they think is the actual quality of the film, and the feelings and opinions of other people. You will hear a lot of them say: 'well you can like that film, but it is objectively bad'. They may not say it explicitly, but that is essentially an insult, and claims that the person is ignoring fact. I am in favour, absolutely, of the subjective experience and perception. The beauty of art consists in its ability to have such manifold effects on people.

I was not suggesting that anyone start with that phrase, but simply that those who wish to present all the findings of their in-depth analyses that is itent on objective illuminatiion, must sum up using that phrase to acknowledge that no amount of comparative analyses ever reaches a point of indisputable or consistent objectivity that everyone can expect to experience.

I do believe there is value in analyses that aims to be objective, as it is how we identify our preferences and learn techniques of art-making.

I don't think we disagree.

>There doesn't seem to me to be anything to suggest that because something is the consensus, or the conventional perspective, that this elevates it beyond subjectivity. 

If a comedy film is trying to be funny, but the general consensus among the target audience is that it *wasn't*, then that provides a basis for a somewhat objective analysis. It's the difference between "here's why *I* didn't find it funny" and "here's why lots of people in the target audience didn't find it funny".

I disagree. Like I said, all that tells us is that a lot of people found the film funny, because a lot of people find the elements within it to be comedic. Objectivity is concerned purely with the thing, the thing independent of the subject. The reaction reflects is a result of the subject, and not the object. I don't even think there is anything wrong with this. I value subjective experience immensely. If a comedy made many people laugh, I suppose that can be considered good. But again arises the problem of the consensus. Many people did not like, and do not like, Fire Walk With Me. Whatever it intended to do, it failed for most people, particularly upon its release. Does this tell us that it is objectively bad?

>If a comedy made many people laugh, I suppose that can be considered good. 

Not good. But if you can confidently say that it achieved its commercial goals, then you can use that as a basis for an analysis. There's a big difference between asking "Why did much of the target audience find this funny?" and "Why is this funny?"


>But again arises the problem of the consensus. Many people did not like, and do not like, Fire Walk With Me. Whatever it intended to do, it failed for most people, particularly upon its release. Does this tell us that it is objectively bad?

It doesn't tell you it's objectively bad. But you could certainly postulate on why it didn't appeal to a wider audience.
